lessons.title: Heat, temperature and heat transfer
lessons.programRef: Form 2 Basic Science — Heat, light, electricity, magnetism (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe how a thermometer works and give the effects of heating.
reviewNotes: Body temperature 37 °C is an average; check whether the syllabus introduces the Kelvin scale (not at this level).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Heat and temperature
blocks.md: **Heat** is energy that flows from a hot object to a cooler one (measured in joules). **Temperature** tells how hot something is (measured in degrees Celsius, °C, with a thermometer). Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C; normal human body temperature is about 37 °C. A liquid-in-glass thermometer works because the liquid **expands** when heated.

blocks.title: Effects of heating
blocks.md: Most solids, liquids and gases **expand** when heated and **contract** when cooled. Railway lines and bridges are built with small gaps for this reason, and power cables are slack in hot weather. Heating can also change the **state** of a substance and raise its temperature.

blocks.caption: Three ways in which heat travels.
blocks.alt: Three pictures: a metal rod heated at one end for conduction, a beaker with rising warm water and sinking cool water for convection, and the Sun sending rays for radiation.

blocks.title: How heat travels
blocks.md:
- **Conduction**: through solids; metals are good **conductors**, wood, plastic and air are **insulators**.
- **Convection**: in liquids and gases; warm fluid is less dense and rises, cool fluid sinks.
- **Radiation**: heat as waves that need no material; it comes from the Sun to Earth. Dark, dull surfaces absorb it well; shiny, light surfaces reflect it.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Heat and temperature are not the same: a bath of warm water holds more heat than a hot cup of tea.
- Convection cannot happen in solids.
- A metal spoon feels colder than wood at the same temperature because it conducts heat from your hand faster.

blocks.title: Why a wooden handle?
blocks.statement: A cooking pot has a metal body and a wooden or plastic handle. Explain.
steps: The metal body is a good conductor so the food heats quickly.
Wood and plastic are insulators, so the handle stays cool to hold.
blocks.answer: Metal conducts heat to the food; the handle insulates the hand.

blocks.title: Name the process
blocks.statement: A room is heated by a fire. The air near the ceiling is warm. Which process carries the heat there and why?
steps: Warm air expands, becomes less dense and rises.
Heat carried by moving air is convection.

objectives: Distinguish luminous and non-luminous objects and describe how shadows form.
Describe the image in a plane mirror.
reviewNotes: Speed of light given as about 300 000 km/s; check the syllabus convention (3 × 10⁸ m/s).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Light travels in straight lines
blocks.md: **Luminous** objects give out their own light (the Sun, a flame, a bulb); **non-luminous** objects such as the Moon are seen because they **reflect** light. Light travels in **straight lines** at about 300 000 km/s (3 × 10⁸ m/s), the fastest speed known. A **shadow** forms when an **opaque** object blocks light. **Transparent** materials let light through (glass); **translucent** ones scatter it (frosted glass).

blocks.caption: Reflection of a ray at a plane mirror.
blocks.alt: A ray hitting a mirror at 40 degrees to the normal and reflecting at 40 degrees on the other side, with the incident ray, reflected ray, normal and angles labelled.

blocks.title: Law of reflection
blocks.md:
The **angle of incidence** (i) equals the **angle of reflection** (r), and both are measured from the **normal**, the line at 90° to the mirror. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in the same plane.

A plane mirror makes an image that is the **same size**, **as far behind the mirror as the object is in front**, upright, and **laterally inverted** (left and right swapped).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Angles are measured from the **normal**, not from the mirror surface.
- The image in a plane mirror cannot be put on a screen: it is virtual.
- The Moon is not luminous: it reflects sunlight.

blocks.title: Find the angle
blocks.statement: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. State the angle of reflection and the angle between the incident and reflected rays.
steps: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 35°.

blocks.title: Distance to the image
blocks.statement: A girl stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is she from her image?
steps: The image is 2 m behind the mirror.

objectives: Draw and describe a simple series circuit and a parallel circuit.
reviewNotes: Ammeter/voltmeter handling is simplified; the sign conventions for current direction are not discussed.
Electrical safety is general advice; follow local rules and a qualified electrician for wiring.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: An electric circuit
blocks.md: A **circuit** is a complete path for **electric current**. It needs a **source** (cell or battery), **conducting wires**, a **load** (bulb) and often a **switch**. The current is measured in **amperes (A)** with an **ammeter** placed in the circuit; the push of the cell is the **voltage**, in **volts (V)**. A break in the path, such as an open switch, stops the current.

blocks.caption: A series circuit: cell, two bulbs and a closed switch.
blocks.alt: A rectangular circuit with a cell on the left, two bulbs on top and a closed switch at the bottom.

blocks.title: Series and parallel
blocks.md: **Series**: components in one loop; the same current flows through all; if one bulb breaks, all go out. **Parallel**: each component has its own branch; if one bulb breaks the other stays on; the **currents in the branches add up**. Houses are wired in parallel. Cells in series add their voltages: three 1.5 V cells give 4.5 V.

blocks.caption: A parallel circuit: two bulbs in separate branches.
blocks.alt: A circuit with a cell, a closed switch and two bulbs each in its own branch between the top and bottom wires.

blocks.title: Conductors and safety
blocks.md: **Conductors** let current pass: metals (copper, aluminium, iron), graphite, salt water. **Insulators** do not: plastic, rubber, glass, dry wood. Safety: never touch bare wires or switches with wet hands; do not overload sockets; do not poke objects into sockets; keep cables away from water; use **fuses** and do not repair mains wiring yourself.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Current is not used up by a bulb: the same current leaves the bulb as enters it in a series loop.
- Pure water is a poor conductor, but tap water and salt water conduct, so water is dangerous near electricity.
- An ammeter goes in the circuit; it is not attached across a cell.

lessons.title: Magnets and magnetism
lessons.programRef: Form 2 Basic Science — Heat, light, electricity, magnetism (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the laws of magnetic poles.
Describe how to make and test a magnet and use a compass.
reviewNotes: Magnet field-line drawing is schematic. Check if the syllabus mentions Earth's magnetic poles naming (geographic vs magnetic).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Magnets and poles
blocks.md: A **magnet** attracts iron and steel. Every magnet has two **poles**, **north (N)** and **south (S)**, where the pull is strongest. A freely hung magnet turns to point north-south. **Like poles repel** (N and N, S and S); **unlike poles attract** (N and S). A broken magnet gives two smaller magnets, each with two poles.

blocks.caption: A bar magnet and its magnetic field lines (simplified).
blocks.alt: A bar magnet with its north pole on the left and south pole on the right, with curved field lines running from north to south around it.

blocks.title: Magnetic materials
blocks.md:
**Magnetic** materials are attracted: **iron, steel, nickel, cobalt**. **Non-magnetic**: copper, aluminium, wood, plastic, glass. Only magnets **repel**, so repulsion is the true test for a magnet; attraction alone could be a piece of iron.

A **compass** has a small magnet needle that points to Earth's magnetic north.

blocks.title: Making and losing magnetism
blocks.md: To **magnetise** a steel needle, stroke it many times in one direction with one pole of a magnet. It can lose its magnetism if it is hammered, heated or dropped many times. Keep magnets in pairs with soft iron **keepers** to stop them weakening. Strong magnets must be kept away from phones, bank cards and watches.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- A magnet does not attract every metal: aluminium and copper are not attracted.
- Attraction does not prove an object is a magnet; repulsion does.
- The north pole of a compass needle points to Earth's magnetic north, which is a south magnetic pole.

blocks.title: Attract or repel?
blocks.statement: The N pole of magnet P is brought near the S pole of magnet Q, then near the N pole of Q. What happens in each case?

blocks.title: Sort the materials
blocks.statement: Sort into magnetic and non-magnetic: iron nail, copper wire, steel pin, plastic ruler.
blocks.answer: Magnetic: iron nail, steel pin. Non-magnetic: copper wire, plastic ruler.
